name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 15 August 1970

clue.text: What a dish for a horse

blocks.note: first meaning: a large flat serving platter
second meaning: a war horse ridden into battle

explanation.surface: Someone marvels at a fine plate of food put out for a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks what dish a horse would eat; the answer is one word naming both a platter and a mount.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an old large meat platter and a cavalry or battle steed.

clue.text: But you needn't be round the bend to live in these streets

definitions.text: But you needn't be round the bend to live in these streets

blocks.clueFragment: But you needn't be round the bend
blocks.note: surface reading: you don't have to be mad
setter's reading: streets that literally curve round in a bend, shaped like a new moon

explanation.surface: Reassurance that living in certain streets doesn't make you crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: Round the bend is slang for mad, but here it describes the curved shape of the street.
explanation.definitionFit: Curved terraces or roads shaped like a sickle moon are commonly named this in British town planning.

clue.text: Where the pontiff might go in van

indicators.note: might hints at a possible state rather than the present one, so the letters can be shifted into another form

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: The Pope could travel in a van, like a modern popemobile.
explanation.walkthrough: The French city housed the popes in the fourteenth century, so it is where a pope might go.
explanation.definitionFit: The papacy was based in this city in southern France during the fourteenth century.

clue.text: Whittier's salad days?

blocks.note: surface reading: the inexperienced youth of the poet Whittier
setter's reading: the middle name of the American poet John Whittier, which also describes salad

explanation.surface: A look back at the poet Whittier's green youthful years.
explanation.walkthrough: Salad days is Shakespeare's phrase for green youth; salad is made of green leaves, which is the poet's middle name.
explanation.definitionFit: John Whittier, the nineteenth-century American poet, had this as his middle name, and lettuce is exactly that.

clue.text: One of those known to the pearl expert?

definitions.text: One of those known to the pearl expert?

blocks.clueFragment: One of those known to the pearl expert?
blocks.note: surface reading: a fact a pearl expert knows
setter's reading: the idiom for an old hand who knows how things work, applied to strands of pearls

explanation.surface: Something only a specialist in pearls would be familiar with.
explanation.walkthrough: An expert is said to know the ropes; a long string of pearls is also called this.
explanation.definitionFit: A long strand of pearls is a jeweller's term for a necklace string, and experts know the ropes idiomatically.

clue.text: Curious ones took Ko-Ko from the county gaol.

definitions.text: Curious ones took Ko-Ko from the county gaol.

blocks.clueFragment: Curious ones took Ko-Ko from the county gaol.
blocks.note: surface reading: some odd people sprang a prisoner from jail
setter's reading: Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado, sings that he was taken from the county jail by a set of curious strokes of luck

explanation.surface: Some odd characters spring a man called Ko-Ko out of the local prison.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Ko-Ko's own account in The Mikado; the curious things that freed him were not people but turns of fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: In the operetta lyric, strokes of fortune, not rescuers, lifted Ko-Ko from prison to high office.

clue.text: Study the poet at work in chatty mood

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase for a participle; 'they were conversing' and 'they were in chatty mood' swap

blocks.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
a poet at work is writing verse

explanation.surface: Someone studies a poet at work while being in the mood to talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Talking informally with others is chatting, the activity of a person in a talkative mood.

clue.text: Scent of a pussyfoot arriving

blocks.note: taken as written
a pussyfoot is a teetotaller, after the American prohibitionist 'Pussyfoot' Johnson; TT is teetotal
ar. is a timetable abbreviation for arriving

explanation.surface: The smell of a stealthy cat creeping in.
explanation.walkthrough: Pussyfoot looks like a cat's tread, but it was a nickname for prohibitionist William Johnson and came to mean a teetotaller.
explanation.definitionFit: This rose oil is a fragrant essence used in perfumery, so it is a scent.

clue.text: There's a strong case for keeping out the water

definitions.text: There's a strong case for keeping out the water

blocks.clueFragment: There's a strong case for keeping out the water
blocks.note: surface reading: a good argument for flood defences
setter's reading: a sturdy watertight chamber used for underwater construction work

explanation.surface: An argument in favour of keeping floodwater out.
explanation.walkthrough: A strong case sounds like a persuasive argument, but it is a literal sturdy box.
explanation.definitionFit: Engineers sink a watertight chamber to let workers build bridge foundations below the river surface.

clue.text: Appears to observe the writing

blocks.note: to observe is to see
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, a piece of writing

explanation.surface: Someone shows up to look at a piece of writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs describe giving an impression or looking a certain way to an observer.

clue.text: That is the law of banishment

blocks.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
lex is Latin for law

explanation.surface: A statement that a certain rule is the legal basis for sending someone away.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no word telling you to rearrange; the old-fashioned setter leaves the jumbling of the two Latin pieces unsignalled.
explanation.definitionFit: Being forced to live away from one's homeland is the standard synonym for being banished.

clue.text: Does its respectable wearer yearn to embrace a tease?

definitions.text: Does its respectable wearer yearn to embrace a tease?

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in one's arms, so one word wraps around the other

blocks.note: to yearn is to pine
strip-tease: a strip is a tease of the undressing kind

explanation.surface: Does the sober city gent in his suit secretly long to hug a strip-tease artist?
explanation.walkthrough: The respectable wearer is the banker or lawyer in a striped suit, and the whole clue doubles as a picture of the cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrow-striped cloth is the classic sober suiting of bankers and lawyers, hence its respectable wearer.

clue.text: Music in the cathedral close

blocks.note: first meaning: pieces where voices enter in turn repeating the same tune
second meaning: clergy attached to a cathedral, who traditionally live in its close

explanation.surface: Music being heard in the grounds around a cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: A cathedral close is the enclosed precinct round a cathedral where its clergy live.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural names both rounds sung in imitation and the chapter clergy of a cathedral living in its precinct.

clue.text: "Strew no more maidens" (Arnold)

blocks.note: surface reading: a strange command to stop scattering young women
setter's reading: a gap-fill from a Matthew Arnold poem, where the missing flowers are the thing not to be strewn

explanation.surface: A quotation from Matthew Arnold that seems to forbid scattering maidens.
explanation.walkthrough: Quotation clues of this era leave out words from a well-known line; the solver supplies the two missing words in front of maidens.
explanation.definitionFit: The flowers of love and mourning fill the gap in the poet's line about scattering blooms.

clue.text: They may not be so popular after the meeting

definitions.text: They may not be so popular after the meeting

blocks.clueFragment: They may not be so popular after the meeting
blocks.note: surface reading: people who lose support after a gathering
setter's reading: a race meeting, after which the horses backed by punters may have lost

explanation.surface: Certain people's popularity may fade once the meeting is over.
explanation.walkthrough: A meeting is a day of horse races; horses strongly fancied beforehand fall from favour if they lose.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the runners most backed by punters before a race, and losing ones lose that support.

clue.text: Momentous, these words?

blocks.note: surface reading: words of great importance
setter's reading: words made up for the moment, used for a single occasion only

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether these are historic, weighty words.
explanation.walkthrough: Momentous is read as 'of the moment' rather than 'important'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lexicographers call a term coined for one particular occasion a nonce word.

clue.text: It sounds agreeable

blocks.note: surface reading: something seems like a pleasant idea
setter's reading: vowel sounds that agree with each other in nearby words

explanation.surface: A casual reply that a suggestion seems fine.
explanation.walkthrough: Sounds turns from a verb (seems) into a noun (speech sounds) that agree.
explanation.definitionFit: The poetic device is a resemblance or chiming of vowel sounds between neighbouring words.

clue.text: A pitcher in which to drown one's sorrows?

definitions.text: A pitcher in which to drown one's sorrows?

blocks.clueFragment: A pitcher in which to drown one's sorrows?
blocks.note: surface reading: a jug of drink for forgetting troubles
setter's reading: the pitcher plant, whose genus is named after the Greek drug that banished grief

explanation.surface: A jug of beer to drink when you want to forget your troubles.
explanation.walkthrough: Nepenthe was the drug of forgetfulness in Homer; the pitcher plant genus borrows the name, and its pitchers drown insects.
explanation.definitionFit: The carnivorous pitcher plant genus is named after the mythical Greek potion that made drinkers forget sorrow.

clue.text: Attic rather than kitchen - sink dramatist!

definitions.text: Attic rather than kitchen - sink dramatist!

blocks.note: surface reading: rooms of a house, the loft versus the kitchen
setter's reading: Attic means of ancient Athens, so a classical Athenian playwright rather than a modern realist one

explanation.surface: A playwright who works in the loft rather than at the kitchen sink.
explanation.walkthrough: Kitchen-sink drama is 1950s British gritty realism; Attic means Athenian, pointing to a Greek tragedian.
explanation.definitionFit: This fifth-century BC Athenian tragedian wrote Medea, a classical playwright of Attica rather than modern realism.

clue.text: Gaberdine?

blocks.note: surface reading: the twill fabric used for raincoats
setter's reading: the older sense of a loose long coarse cloak, a garment of woollen cloth

explanation.walkthrough: Stuff is an old word for woollen fabric, and a stuff gown is also what a junior barrister wears in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaberdine was historically a long loose robe of coarse woollen cloth, which is exactly a gown made of stuff.

clue.text: Fabulous formation of horses

blocks.note: first meaning: a creature of fable, the one-horned beast
second meaning: a carriage team of three horses, two side by side with one leading

explanation.surface: A splendid display of horses arranged in formation.
explanation.walkthrough: Fabulous here means existing only in fables, and stands for the legendary creature.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary horned beast of myth shares its name with a three-horse coaching team arrangement.

clue.text: Conundrum in a fine burst of prose

indicators.note: something that bursts is blown apart, so the following word scatters into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzle set out in an outburst of fine writing.
explanation.definitionFit: A baffling question or riddle that is hard to answer is a conundrum.

clue.text: Bearing the mark of a literary butterfly

blocks.note: first meaning: printed or impressed with a seal or postmark
second meaning: Kipling's Just So story The Butterfly That ___

explanation.surface: Something carries the marking of a butterfly from a book.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's Just So Stories include a tale of a butterfly that brought its foot down hard on the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: The participle means impressed with a seal or mark, and it describes what Kipling's butterfly did.

clue.text: "Nor all that gold" (Gray)

blocks.note: surface reading: an incomplete phrase about gold
setter's reading: Thomas Gray's cat ode ends that not all that shines is gold, and the missing verb fills the gap

explanation.surface: A fragment of Thomas Gray's verse about gold.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray's Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat closes with the proverb in an old form; the solver supplies the missing verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic verb meaning sparkles or shines completes the old proverb that shining things are not always gold.

clue.text: "But a man's reach should exceed his — (Browning)

definitions.text: "But a man's reach should exceed his — (Browning)

blocks.clueFragment: But a man's reach should exceed his
blocks.note: surface reading: an unfinished line about ambition
setter's reading: the famous closing word of Robert Browning's line in Andrea del Sarto fills the dash

explanation.surface: Browning's line that people should aim beyond what they can hold.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line continues 'or what's a heaven for?'; the solver supplies the missing word at the dash.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the hold or extent of one's hands, the limit ambition should strive past.

clue.text: There's no membership of this body

definitions.text: There's no membership of this body

blocks.clueFragment: There's no membership of this body
blocks.note: surface reading: an organisation that has no members
setter's reading: members are limbs, and this body is a trunk without arms or legs

explanation.surface: A club or committee that admits nobody.
explanation.walkthrough: Body and member are both read anatomically: a member is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: A sculpture or human trunk without head, arms or legs is a body lacking limbs.

clue.text: Pitchers get to work in the field

definitions.text: Pitchers get to work in the field

blocks.clueFragment: Pitchers get to work in the field
blocks.note: surface reading: bowlers or baseball pitchers start playing
setter's reading: people pitching tents, who set up camp in a field

explanation.surface: The bowlers or baseball throwers take the field and start their game.
explanation.walkthrough: Pitchers are not sportsmen but campers putting up tents.
explanation.definitionFit: To set up a camp of tents in an open place is what pitching tents in a field amounts to.

clue.text: A simple remedy

blocks.note: surface reading: an easy cure
setter's reading: a simple is an old noun for a medicinal plant used on its own

explanation.surface: An easy home cure for an ailment.
explanation.walkthrough: Simple is read as the old noun for a single medicinal plant, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Healers once used single medicinal plants called simples, so a plant cure is this.

clue.text: "Just a little love, a little kiss" perhaps

definitions.text: "Just a little love, a little kiss" perhaps

blocks.clueFragment: "Just a little love, a little kiss"
blocks.note: surface reading: the title line of a sentimental old song
setter's reading: a word for a slight, passing love affair, built on the French for love with a diminutive ending

explanation.surface: A line from a sentimental old love song.
explanation.walkthrough: The French ending -ette makes things small, so the word is literally a little love.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived word means a trifling or brief love affair, a minor romance.

clue.text: Was optimistic like founder of Ruritania

blocks.note: first meaning: looked forward expectantly
second meaning, a pun: in the manner of Anthony Hope, who invented the kingdom of Ruritania in The Prisoner of Zenda

explanation.surface: Someone looked on the bright side, just as the creator of a fictional kingdom did.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruritania is the imaginary country of Anthony Hope's novel; adding -ed to his surname makes a playful adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking forward expectantly to a good outcome is past-tense wishing; the pun reads it as the novelist's name plus a suffix.

clue.text: Flags for the Lancers

blocks.note: surface reading: banners for a cavalry regiment or the Lancers dance
setter's reading: small pointed flags carried on the end of a lance

explanation.surface: Banners being handed out to a cavalry regiment.
explanation.definitionFit: These are long narrow triangular streamers traditionally fixed to a knight's or cavalryman's lance.

clue.text: There's more to it than just team exhortations

blocks.clueFragment: There's more to it than just team exhortations
blocks.note: surface reading: a situation is more complicated than pep talks
setter's reading: split in two, the answer is a rallying cry telling players to be teams

explanation.surface: Winning takes more than a coach shouting encouragement at the players.
explanation.walkthrough: Sides are teams, so a shout of 'Be sides!' is a team exhortation; joined up it means moreover.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means moreover or in addition, which is what saying there is more to it implies.
